documents.title: Generative AI in the Classroom
documents.summary: Teaching-center guide applying the Student Code of Conduct to AI: unauthorized or uncited AI use is an integrity violation, detectors are not recommended, and instructors get assignment-design ideas to discourage or incorporate AI. It also points to syllabus language and consultation.
documents.stance_why: The page states the integrity policy "already prohibits the use of unauthorized resources, including AI content generators" and treats unauthorized AI as assistance violating the Student Code, so AI is banned unless the instructor authorizes it; it offers no tiers or templates, though it also suggests instructors may integrate AI.

units.why: The page's headline conclusion says the integrity policy covers AI: "already prohibits the use of unauthorized resources, including AI content generators". It binds students and fits P36 (AI as an unauthorized resource handled under integrity rules) better than P01 because the ban is conditional on authorization.
units.anchor: academic integrity policy already prohibits the use of unauthorized resources, including AI content generators
units.frag_start: Illinois State’s academic integrity policy already

units.why: The Center says it updated the suggested syllabus statement to mention AI. This is a fact about communicating expectations through the syllabus, so P09; it is not a mandate, hence informs.
units.anchor: the Center has updated the
units.frag_start: Illinois State’s academic integrity policy already
units.policy: The Center has updated its suggested academic integrity syllabus statement to note that the academic integrity policy prohibits unauthorized resources including AI content generators.

units.why: Detection is described as unsolved: "There is not yet a detection service that can definitively determine" authorship. This is a factual statement that detectors cannot be relied on, so P39, informing instructors.
units.anchor: There is not yet a detection service that can definitively determine whether content was produced
units.frag_start: There is not yet a detection
units.frag_end: are still in the early stages of development

units.why: Instructors are told they "should never put their students’ work into services that claim to be able to detect" AI, citing privacy and IP. P50 (protect personal data) fits better than P39 because the stated reason is privacy and consent. Modality is should-not ('should never').

units.frag_start: Due to concerns about student privacy
units.policy: Instructors should never put their students’ work into AI-detection services or into generative AI services without their students’ informed consent.

units.why: The center states "we cannot recommend their use" of AI detectors because none is vetted by peer-reviewed study. This is advice against relying on detectors, so P39.

units.why: Guidance says the Student Code of Conduct covers "unauthorized use of any resource or service not authorized by or acknowledged to the instructor", which includes AI. This classifies unauthorized AI use as an integrity violation: P36.

units.policy: Instructors who suspect AI-generated work should follow the same process as for any other academic integrity concern, as laid out by Student Conduct and Community Responsibilities.

units.why: The page says syllabus language "can be added to your course syllabus and discussed with your students". It is optional advice to communicate expectations; P09 is the nearest type, but the modality is weaker (should/may) than the type's 'must'.
units.anchor: This language can be added to your course syllabus and discussed with your students

units.why: Advice to "connect your assignment prompts deeply to in-class discussions" so AI content has less value. An assignment redesign around AI: P35.
units.anchor: Consider connecting your assignment prompts deeply to in-class discussions and activities
units.frag_end: negates the value of AI-created content

units.why: "Require more than one draft of the same paper/assignment" is a redesign (multi-pass) to discourage AI use: P35.
units.anchor: Require more than one draft of the same paper/assignment

units.why: "Encourage primary research" so work uses information not on the internet is an assignment redesign around AI: P35.

units.why: Instructors should "Develop writing prompts ... that require higher-level cognitive engagement" per Bloom's Taxonomy to resist AI: P35.
units.anchor: that require higher-level cognitive engagement
units.policy: Instructors develop writing prompts and other assignments at levels of Bloom's Taxonomy that require higher-level cognitive engagement, because AI content is often lacking in complexity and depth for analyze, apply, understand and remember tasks.

units.why: "Use small assignments/papers ... to allow them to be written during class time" shifts work to in-class, unassisted settings: P33.
units.anchor: to allow them to be written during class time
units.policy: Instructors use small assignments or papers, with other technologies such as a Canvas quiz or a Nearpod prompt, so that they are written during class time.

units.policy: Instructors may allow students to bring an AI-generated draft to class and use it as a first draft to correct, expand and improve.

documents.title: Ethical Use of Generative AI (thesis, dissertation, capstone, comprehensive exams)
documents.summary: Graduate School statement for theses, dissertations, capstones and comprehensive exams. AI use is allowed within disciplinary guidelines but must be disclosed to the committee and cited; unauthorized use may violate Policy 1.8.
documents.stance_why: The statement says AI "can support innovative and creative scholarship when used within appropriate guidelines" and then requires disclosure to the committee and citation, so AI is permitted with conditions.

units.why: The statement says generative AI "can support innovative and creative scholarship when used within appropriate guidelines". AI is allowed with conditions: P02 (permit by default), conditioned on discipline guidelines.
